segments.caption: A vertical log hive, inoculated with propolis and beeswax and mounted 10 feet high in a tree, is shown as a swarm of bees moves in on April 4, 2013, beginning their new life in the structure.

The video shows a person documenting the early stages of a tree surgery or modification, focusing on a large, mature tree with a rough, textured bark. The camera pans upward, revealing a significant, cleanly cut opening in the trunk, which appears to be a deliberate modification. A hand then enters the frame, pointing to the freshly cut surface, which is secured with a braided rope. Text overlaid on the image indicates this is the "First opening," captured six days after the

A person carefully opens a circular wooden panel, secured with rope, to reveal the interior of a tree trunk. The first frame, dated April 10, 2013, shows the "first opening" six days after an event referred to as "birth." The subsequent frames provide close-up views of the rough, textured wood inside, showing small holes and indentations, suggesting the presence of a hidden creature or the aftermath of a natural process. A close-up view reveals a dense cluster of dark-colored bees actively swarming and moving over a rough wooden surface, with some bees visible on the surrounding wood, indicating a hive or nest within a wooden structure.
A person opens a tree cavity 17 days after the "birth" of a colony to reveal a dense mass of dark, newly emerged bees, indicating the successful development and emergence of a new bee swarm.

The frames show a close-up view inside a wooden structure, revealing a large, dense cluster of bees actively forming and maintaining a swarm or hive within the confined space. The bees are tightly packed, covering the surface of what appears to be a natural or man-made comb, with visible wax structures. The scene captures the persistent, collective movement and organization of the colony as it settles into its new location, highlighting the industrious nature of the bees as they establish their new home.

A close-up view of a dense swarm of bees clustered around a tree cavity, followed by shots of the tree’s entrance hole and a cut section with a rope tied across, indicating a managed beekeeping or hive relocation effort.
A person pulls a rope taut across a freshly cut tree stump, revealing a dense swarm of bees packed tightly inside the hollow cavity, indicating the rope was used to access or extract the hive.

A bee swarm, dense and active, clings to the interior of a wooden structure, likely a hive or box, as a person’s hand later ties a rope around a tree trunk, marking the fourth opening of the hive 11 weeks after its “birth” on June 22, 2013.

A person’s hand is shown interacting with a rope tied around a tree, which has a large, circular opening carved into its trunk. The hand manipulates the rope and then presses against the exposed wood inside the opening, suggesting the person is inspecting or demonstrating the condition of the tree, which appears to be part of a long-term project or experiment, as indicated by the text overlay referencing “Forth opening” and a date 11 weeks after “birth.”
A person carefully removes a section of bark from a hollow in a large tree, revealing a dense swarm of bees packed tightly inside the cavity.

A beekeeper carefully extracts a large, natural tree cavity swarm from a pine tree, revealing a dense cluster of bees inside, and then holds the hollowed-out section to inspect the colony before removing it from the tree.

A close-up view reveals a large, natural beehive nestled inside a hollow tree trunk, with thick ropes securing the tree. The camera peers into the cavity, showing a dense, bustling colony of bees actively tending to their honeycomb structures, which are partially visible through the swarm. The bees move rapidly across the comb, indicating a thriving, active hive within the tree.
A dense swarm of bees actively moves across and around honeycomb frames inside a wooden hive, their constant motion highlighting the hive’s bustling, living core.
A person gently probes a dense cluster of bees within a natural, wooden hive, revealing the active, honeycomb-laden interior where the insects swarm over and around the hexagonal wax cells.

A close-up view of a bustling beehive, showing worker bees actively tending to honeycomb cells, with a glimpse into a darker, cluttered interior cavity of the hive, followed by abrupt transitions to a textured, aged paper background and then complete darkness.
